documents.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is being integrated into medical education globally, yet evidence from sub-Saharan Africa remains sparse. Postgraduate medical training institutions in this region face distinctive cultural, resource and infrastructure constraints that may shape how educators and trainees engage with AI. This study examined knowledge and self-reported use of AI among postgraduate medical residents and faculty in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted across three postgraduate medical training universities in Dar es Salaam the Aga Khan University (AKU), Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (MUHAS), and Hubert Kairuki Memorial University (HKMU). A census sampling approach was used, targeting all available residents and faculty. Data was collected via an online structured questionnaire assessing AI knowledge, exposure, and self-rated competence. Knowledge scores were derived from a ten-item questionnaire and compared across groups using Welch's t-test and multivariable linear regression to determine association with knowledge scores. Results A total of 155 participants participated in the study (116 residents, 39 faculty). Mean age group was 31–40 years. Formal AI training was rare (7.1%), yet 80.0% reported using AI in teaching or learning activities. Residents used AI substantially more than faculty (65.8% vs. 14.2%). Overall objective knowledge was moderate (mean score 59.0%, SD 18.2%), with no significant difference between residents and faculty (p = 0.623). Specialty was also associated with knowledge scores, with medical and radiology specialties outperforming non-clinical specialties Self-rated knowledge at Level 5 was the only independent predictor of higher objective scores in multivariable analysis (β = 0.151; 95% CI 0.022–0.302; p = 0.049). Conclusions AI use is widespread among postgraduate trainees in Dar es Salaam despite minimal formal training. Knowledge gaps are evident, particularly around foundational AI concepts. Self-perceived competence, rather than professional role or formal training, predicted objective knowledge. These findings underscore the need for structured, contextually adapted AI literacy curricula within postgraduate medical education in Tanzania and similar settings.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Rising imaging workload and a shortage of radiology specialists have driven interest in artificial intelligence (AI) to improve diagnostic speed and accuracy. This systematic review, without meta-analysis, describes how AI affects diagnostic accuracy and operational efficiency compared with human interpretation in diagnostic radiology. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) and Cochrane guidance, PubMed, ClinicalKey, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar were searched on 11 April 2026 for studies published from January 2019 onwards. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and a Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2)-based risk-of-bias assessment. Twenty-one studies were included: 11 compared standalone AI with human readers, six compared AI-assisted with unassisted readers, and four reported both; 18 evaluated task-specific image-analysis AI and three evaluated generative AI models. Because no subgroup was homogeneous enough to pool, we synthesised results narratively and stratified them by comparison type, AI category, imaging modality, and study quality. Standalone image-analysis AI achieved high sensitivity for fractures and selected chest findings but performed less well on subtle findings and lower-quality images, and in one computed tomography-referenced comparison a radiologist outperformed AI. AI assistance improved reader performance more consistently, particularly among less experienced readers. Generative models did not reach specialist performance on complex tasks. Efficiency gains were concentrated in normal studies, and the only randomised trial found lower mammography screen-reading workload with similar early screening performance. No study assessed patient outcomes, and 18 of 21 studies were retrospective. This evidence supports AI only as a supervised, complementary tool; improvements in diagnostic accuracy should not be equated with clinical benefit.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an important tool in social media marketing, enabling businesses to deliver personalized content and enhance consumer engagement. At the same time, growing environmental awareness has increased interest in green products. This study develops a conceptual framework to explain the relationship between AI-driven social media marketing, consumer trust, and green purchase intention in Uzbekistan. Based on recent literature, the proposed framework suggests that AI-driven social media marketing strengthens consumer trust and positively influences consumers' intention to purchase green products. The study contributes to the green marketing literature by integrating these constructs into a unified conceptual model and provides a theoretical foundation for future empirical research in Uzbekistan. RU Искусственный интеллект (ИИ) стал важным инструментом маркетинга в социальных сетях, позволяя компаниям предоставлять персонализированный контент и повышать вовлечённость потребителей. In Outcome-Based Education (OBE) environments, student academic progressionrepresents a complex, non-linear dynamic system governed by multi-faceted indicatorsincluding performance trajectories, engagement metrics, and learningsupport mechanisms. Traditional evaluation methods often fail to capture time-dependentperformance risks and degradation patterns across successive assessmentstages. In this paper, we establish a novel reliability-based degradationmodeling framework that adapts engineering reliability principles and hazard-ratesurvival analysis to educational decision-support systems. Utilizing a standardized,publicly available academic progress dataset, our framework modelsperformance stability via cumulative reliability functions and identifies critical vulnerabilitythresholds using hazard-rate formulations. Students are classified intodistinct progression cohorts (high, moderate, and low achievers) based on normalizedperformance distributions. Empirical findings demonstrate a strong correlationbetween early academic stability and long-term progression reliability,showing that multi-year failing trajectories exhibit exponentially higher degradationrates. The proposed framework provides an interpretable, data-driven analyticaltool to monitor student risk, support early Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driveninterventions, and optimize institutional decision-making in modern outcome-based learning architectures.

As arts in transit has become an increasingly prominent practice in urban public transportation spaces worldwide, it is important to understand how AI-generated images are reshaping visual orders across different urban contexts. Taking Beijing Metro Line 2 as the primary case, supplemented by contextual observations on Lines 1, 4, and 10, this study draws on participant observation and semi-structured interviews. The findings reveal three interconnected changes. First, traditional transit art continues to provide durable cultural references, yet it faces growing competition from rapidly renewed visual content for limited passenger attention, producing a form of attentional displacement. Second, generative AI accelerates an already commercialized visual regime by lowering production costs, shortening revision cycles, increasing scalability, and redistributing authorship across algorithms, designers, and managers. Third, AI-generated imagery has expanded from advertising into public-service communication and cultural content, where it is incorporated into existing processes of institutional review and display. These changes reveal two dimensions of visual governance: institutional control over the production and display of visual content, and the organization of attention and spatial meaning through visual means. The Beijing Metro case therefore reconsiders the public value of arts in transit by showing how AI-driven visual production is reconfiguring the institutional, cultural, and perceptual conditions through which publicness is produced in urban transit space.

This article discusses examples from the field of special machine construction that feature a high degree of automation. Systems for the testing methods UT, MT, and PT are presented. Either component handling is automated via robotics or gantry systems, or sensor positioning is automated in the case of ultrasonic testing. In ultrasonic testing, fully automated evaluation has long been state of the art. Current trends include phased array testing (PAUT), using modern algorithms such as TFM (Total Focusing Method) or PWI (Plane Wave Imaging) when appropriate. In magnetic particle testing, the crack evaluation is usually carried out manually. The AI-based software CRACKVIEW AI is now used for fully automated crack assessment. The algorithm has been trained using many thousands of images and delivers good results. Initial results for PT testing are now available. The special machine construction sector is undergoing change due to the increased use of robotics. High flexibility and falling prices are driving this development. High labour costs, the difficulty in finding suitable inspection staff, and the desire to minimise the "human factor" are further drivers behind an increasing trend towards a higher degree of automation.

documents.abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this paper is to examine the use of digital platforms to automate financial and management accounting functions, with particular focus on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain technology. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study adopts a qualitative secondary data research methodology using existing scholarly materials, industry reports, and case studies to evaluate the effectiveness of these technologies in improving accounting operations. The sample of 27 publications (2014–2026) was obtained from online academic databases such as Google Scholar, ScienceDirect and JSTOR, and examined by thematic analysis. Research Limitation: The study identifies high implementation costs, technical complexity, and data privacy and cybersecurity issues as the main challenges, indicating the need for further research on scalable and cost-effective solutions. Findings: The findings indicate that AI-driven automation enhances precision, reduces human error, and supports more accurate decision-making through instant data analysis. Blockchain technology increases the transparency, security, and reliability of financial transactions through its decentralised and immutable structure. Practical Implication: The adoption of AI and blockchain in accounting systems offers considerable advantages for organisations, particularly in improving operational efficiency and supporting strategic management. Social Implication: The wider adoption of digital technologies contributes to more transparent, secure, and reliable accounting practices in the modern business environment. Originality/Value: The article examines AI and blockchain in management accounting tasks, such as forecasting and decision support, which have received less attention than auditing and financial reporting, and highlights future research directions for the development of scalable solutions that can be adopted at lower cost.

Abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence, especially Generative AI, is really changing how we work and what employment looks like. While these AI technologies can boost productivity and enhance decision-making, they might also lessen the need for human workers in some roles, leading to layoffs and job losses. This shift has sparked worries about job security, potential layoffs, the need for reskilling, and whether current labor laws are adequate. This research examines whether the safeguards provide under Chapter V-B of the Industrial Disputes Act from 1947 are enough to protect employees whose jobs are impacted by automation and tech advancements. It zooms in on key legal protections related to layoffs, notice periods, compensation, required government approvals, and other employee safeguards. Additionally, it looks at the challenges posed by Generative AI, especially how tech changes can shift job roles, cut down the demand for certain skills, or even render some positions obsolete. The study takes a doctrinal and qualitative approach, pulling from a variety of sources like legislation, court rulings, academic research, government documents, and insights into AI, automation, and employment. It also examines the Industrial Relations Code of 2020 to grasp how India's labor law framework is evolving in light of technology. The findings indicate that while current labor laws do offer crucial protections during layoffs, they might not fully tackle the issues brought on by AI-related job changes. There's a strong suggestion that more focus is needed on reskilling, redeploying, transparency, and providing support during transitions before any layoffs occur. Therefore, the study advocates for a more employee-centered approach, encouraging employers to prioritize reskilling and redeployment ahead of layoffs, while also balancing tech advancements, business demands, and employee rights. 1. Introduction With the rapid growth of large language models (LLMs) and the AI-related industry, AI systems have come to core industrial and economic infrastructures. However, an appropriate redistribution structure for "knowledge creation" (such as academic papers and intellectual property)—which forms the foundation of AI learning and inference—and an autonomous mechanism connecting AI economic revenues to external social security and cultural redistributions have not yet been established. In this study, we propose the "Casino Protocol," a smart contract protocol that automatically collects a flat 1% from the revenue of AI-related companies and uses it as the source for "cultural redistribution (artist fees)," "autonomous driving insurance reserves" as social infrastructure, and "tuition fees (knowledge rewards)" for academic achievements (DOIs) and the origin node.

documents.abstract: Background: Low back pain (LBP) is a major occupational health problem among informal sector workers, particularly fishing community members who perform repetitive and physically demanding tasks with limited ergonomic support. In Indonesia, coastal fishing communities often have inadequate access to occupational health services Objective: To assess the prevalence and severity of LBP among fishing community workers in Sukolilo Baru, Bulak, Surabaya, and evaluate the effect of a structured Back Pain Exercise (BPE) intervention combined with health education on pain intensity. Methods: A community-based cross-sectional study with a pre–post intervention evaluation was conducted among 35 workers recruited through purposive sampling following STROBE and TIDieR guidelines. The intervention consisted of a structured health education session and a supervised BPE programme, with pain intensity measured using the Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS 0–10). Results: LBP prevalence was 91.4% (n = 32), with 62.5% reporting moderate pain and 37.5% reporting mild pain. Following the intervention, all LBP-positive participants demonstrated a reduction in pain intensity (median NPRS decreased from 5.0 to 3.0; p < 0.001). Multivariate logistic regression identified work duration ?8 hours/day (aOR 4.82; 95% CI: 1.94–11.98; p = 0.001), frequent heavy lifting (aOR 3.91; 95% CI: 1.42–10.74; p = 0.008), and non-ergonomic posture (aOR 3.44; 95% CI: 1.21–9.77; p = 0.020) Conclusion: BPE combined with structured health education is a feasible and effective non-pharmacological approach for reducing LBP severity in coastal informal work settings. Community-based occupational health programmes targeting ergonomic risk factors should be integrated into primary healthcare networks for vulnerable maritime workers.

documents.abstract: Background: Among the health related problems, commercial sex is one of the leading occupational health problems in Bangladesh. To understand the health risks among female sex workers is very important. This risks may be due to work related problems and others. This study was done to understand the socio demographic profile, background of commercial sex and health related problems among the female sex workers. Materials and methods: The study was a cross-sectional study conducted during the period from 6th to 31st March 2026. A purposive sampling technique was applied to select 69 female sex workers and data were collected by face to face interview using a structured questionnaire. Obtained results were compiled and analyzed using SPSS version 23. Chi square test was done to see the association between socio demographic problem and background of commercial sex. Results: Among the 69 sex workers, 58(84.05%) respondents were aged between 25 to 40 years. Muslims were predominant in this study which constituted about 46(66.7%). Majority 60(87%) of the respondents were married. 38(55.1%) had primary level of education, 19(27.5%) were illiterate, 52(75.4%) came from nuclear family and 37(53.7%) belonged to lower middle class. 47(68.1%) had income ranging from TK. 20,000 to 50,000. Among the 69 study subjects, 55(79.7%) had joined in sex work at the age of 18-25 years and 14(20.3%) had started at the age of 25-40 years. 35(50.7%) were in this work for 1-5 years and 34(49.3%) were working for more than 5 years. All 69 were involved in other profession earlier. Regarding number of clients, it was seen that 21(30.4%) had 2 clients per day, 45(65.2%) had 3-5 clients and 3(4.3%) had more than 5 clients per day. All 69 respondents were involved in other professions. 38(55.1%) said they quitted previous job due to bad working condition, 9(13%) for personal issues, 8(11.6%) for family problems and 14(20.3%) for less income. 32(46.4%) joined sex work at their own wish, 30(43.5%) due to more income and 7(10.1%) were cheated and trapped in this profession. All the respondents of the current study knew about sexually transmitted diseases. 5(7%) suffered from hepatitis and 17(25%) suffered from scabies. 52(75.4%) said that they had a guilty feeling for joining sex work and 53(77%) wanted to quit sex. Conclusion: This study concluded that female sex workers got involved in sex work for more income and low socioeconomic status. Socio demographic factors were sensible to develop health risks. Increasing awareness and educational support might help to reduce the work-related health risks among female sex workers. IAHS Medical Journal Vol 9(1), June 2026; 39-43

The article deals with the lexical and stylistic analysis of three essays generated by artificial intelligence and one essay by a human author on the same topic. The differences in the lexical and expressive means that convey emotionality, evaluation, and the degree of subjectivity have been revealed. The functional styles of each essay produced by artificial intelligence have been identified. The conclusion is made that artificial intelligence does not draw clear boundaries between styles and genres of texts, between essays, in particular, for example, between the publicistic and literary styles, or between the colloquial and literary styles. It is claimed that at the current stage of the artificial intelligence development and application in generating texts of different styles, the problem lies in the AI’s failure to distinguish between functional styles and text genres. AI cannot generate words based on cultural, literary, linguistic, and other associations related to word play in the way a human can.

Abstract Interactive digital resources are widely used in anatomy education, but their development typically requires programming expertise or commercial software, and pre-existing resources may not match an educator’s specific teaching requirements. Large language models (LLMs) are now capable of generating functional web code from conversational prompts, creating the possibility of educators producing their own interactive simulations without programming experience. Using LLMs to generate simulations for anatomical education, rather than as tutoring or assessment aids, remains under-investigated. This brief report is a proof-of-concept workflow in which three LLM platforms (OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini, and Anthropic Claude) were provided with reviewed anatomy content and prompted to generate interactive, browser-based simulations. Ten single-file Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) simulations were produced covering cranial nerve lesion testing, the pupillary light and corneal reflexes, extraocular muscle testing, visual field defects, spinal cord syndromes, the circle of willis, and the urinary sphincter function system. The simulations incorporate AI (Artificial Intelligence)-generated anatomical images, adjustable lesion parameters, and scenario-based clinical reasoning. Iterative refinement was necessary to achieve accurate results, as the AI repeatedly made errors, including confusion between left and right orientations, inaccurate positioning of facial features, and the occasional generation of images instead of modifying the code as instructed. These challenges required multiple rounds of correction and careful human oversight to ensure the final output met the intended requirements. Preliminary simulation assessment and comments from Medicine Year 2 colleagues, Oxford AI Build club, learning technologist, Teaching demonstrators were encouraging regarding clarity and engagement, although no formal student evaluation of learning outcomes has yet been conducted. We conclude that LLMs can translate structured anatomical knowledge into functional interactive anatomy simulations and describe a replicable workflow, while emphasising that expert review remains indispensable.

documents.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) extends conventional predictive and generative AI by enabling systems to pursue goals through reasoning, planning, information retrieval, memory, tool use, and interaction with clinical workflows. These capabilities create new opportunities for medicine but also a distinct evaluation problem: the reliability of an agent cannot be inferred from the accuracy of its underlying model or final answer alone. Errors may arise during information retrieval, tool use, state updates, inter-agent communication, or autonomous action and may propagate across a clinical workflow. This critical review examines approaches for evaluating and clinically validating agentic AI in medicine. Existing frameworks, including TRIPOD+AI, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, DECIDE-AI, STARD-AI, FUTURE-AI, and Good Machine Learning Practice, provide important foundations but were not primarily designed for systems with persistent state, repeated actions, tool use, and multi-agent interaction. Emerging agent benchmarks increasingly address interactive tasks, tool use, trajectory reliability, and adversarial testing. We propose a five-level evaluation framework spanning model, agent, trajectory, system, and clinical outcome, together with a clinical validation ladder progressing from component testing and simulation to retrospective evaluation, prospective silent deployment, supervised clinical use, bounded action, and post-deployment surveillance. Key gaps include standardized trajectory metrics, evaluation of correlated multi-agent errors, autonomy-aware validation, human–agent performance, and lifecycle monitoring. Radiotherapy is used as a high-stakes clinical exemplar. We argue that agentic AI should be evaluated as a dynamic sociotechnical system and that clinical evidence must extend beyond accuracy toward behavioral reliability, safety, and demonstrated clinical benefit.

documents.abstract: Purpose – A counterfactual explanation for Indonesian text classification must simultaneously flip the classifier’s decision, remain a minimal and fluent edit, and preserve content that has no bearing on the label. This study asks whether a more powerful generator yields a better Indonesian counterfactual and benchmarks five generators under a single multi-criteria framework. Design/methods/approach – Five generators, a masked-language substitution baseline, two zero-shot LLM pipelines, a gradient-guided variant, and a second-family LLM, were evaluated on two Indonesian test sets across validity, edit quality, format compliance, and cost, combined into a single composite index, and tested for statistical significance. Findings: The masked-language baseline is the strongest and cheapest generator, leading on both flip rate and composite quality while running approximately 55 to 198 times faster than the LLM pipelines. The LLM pipelines are competitive on edit quality but not on validity, and the second-family model degenerates on roughly two-thirds of its outputs, a failure that a flip-rate-only evaluation would have masked. Research implications/limitations: For practitioners building trustworthy AI systems, the practical implication is that a cheaper, simpler generator can be a safer choice, and that generator selection should rest on multi-axis, cost-aware evidence rather than on flip rate or model size alone. All axes here are automated proxies evaluated on two tasks without human judgement. Originality/value – To the best of our knowledge, this study presents the first multicriteria counterfactual benchmark for Indonesian text classification, showing that generator size is a poor proxy for explanation quality and offering a reusable, cost-aware protocol for selecting trustworthy counterfactual methods in lower-resourced languages.

documents.abstract: This review examines research on the integration of Edge Computing and Blockchain, with a focus on how this integration can enhance security, trust, and decentralization while maintaining low latency and acceptable performance. The review covers integration architectures, smart contracts, identity management and access control, trust management, resource management and task offloading, as well as major applications in the Internet of Things, industrial and healthcare environments, smart cities, and connected vehicles. It also discusses key challenges related to limited edge resources, consensus latency, storage, scalability, and privacy. The literature indicates a shift toward lightweight, adaptive, and hybrid solutions that combine the processing speed of the edge with the trust and auditability of Blockchain, supported by smart contracts, suitable consensus mechanisms, sharding, and artificial intelligence to improve system efficiency.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: This study examines the determinants of ethical artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among university students by integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and Digital Divide Theory. Specifically, this study investigates the effects of digital literacy, social influence, and digital divide on ethical AI adoption, as well as the moderating role of digital divide in the relationships between digital literacy, social influence, and ethical AI adoption. A quantitative survey was conducted involving 408 university students in Indonesia. The data were analyzed using regression analysis, supported by reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, Gaussian copula endogeneity check, Harman’s single-factor test, non-response bias test, and simple slope analysis. The findings show that digital literacy has a positive and significant effect on ethical AI adoption, indicating that students with stronger digital literacy are more likely to use AI critically, responsibly, and in accordance with academic integrity. Social influence also has a positive and significant effect, suggesting that lecturers, peers, academic norms, and institutional guidance play an important role in encouraging responsible AI use. Digital divide-related conditions are also significantly associated with ethical AI adoption, highlighting the importance of access, capability, and digital support in AI-supported learning. However, the moderating effects of digital divide are not statistically supported. These findings suggest that digital divide functions more as a direct contextual factor than as a moderating variable. This study contributes to the literature on AI adoption in higher education by emphasizing that ethical AI adoption is shaped by individual digital competence, social-academic support, and inclusive digital conditions. The findings also imply that universities need to strengthen digital literacy, develop clear AI-use guidelines, and reduce digital access gaps to promote ethical and inclusive AI adoption.

Search and discovery on the 2026 internet is broken for three groups: users who want to find real businesses and resources, small businesses who want to be found, and honest affiliate operators who want to earn from genuine recommendations. Search engines rank results by signals that reward scale, not quality. A local hardware store cannot outrank a content farm that produces ten thousand SEO-optimized pages per day with large language models. Paying for search advertising puts small businesses into bidding wars against companies with orders-of-magnitude larger budgets. Social media demands constant content production — videos, posts, engagement farming — work that has nothing to do with the actual service the business provides. Review platforms are corrupted. Fake reviews, review bombing, pay-to-play visibility schemes, and extortion dynamics have made star ratings unreliable. Users append "reddit" to their search queries as a trust signal, but Reddit itself is degrading as it monetizes and as marketers infiltrate communities. AI answer engines attempt to solve the problem by synthesizing responses, but they draw from the same polluted index and introduce hallucination risk. The underlying data is compromised. No amount of summarization fixes a contaminated source. Honest affiliate operators face the same structural disadvantage. An operator who genuinely tests products and recommends what they believe in cannot compete on volume against content farms that rewrite product descriptions and stuff affiliate links without touching the products. The algorithm cannot distinguish the two. The content farm wins on output volume every time. Three intermediaries sit between a person and a useful resource: algorithmic ranking that rewards manipulation, centralized moderation that makes uniform visibility decisions for all users, and review systems that are themselves a manipulation surface. All three are failing.

Objective We examined self-reported work-related injury and its association with ergonomic stressors among municipal solid waste collectors in The Gambia. Methods In a 2020 cross-sectional survey at Brikama Area Council (n=98) and Kanifing Municipal Council (n=107), we modelled the number of anatomical regions with a reported injury over 12 months (0 to 9) against a six-item ergonomic stressor count (0 to 6), using Poisson regression with robust standard errors; binary outcomes used modified Poisson regression. The outcome is an injury-site count, not a musculoskeletal disorder measure. Reporting followed STROBE. Results Work-related injury was reported by 93.2% of workers (95% CI 88.9 to 95.9) and injury in three or more regions by 78.0% (71.9 to 83.2; mean 4.27, SD 2.18). Each additional stressor was associated with a 14% higher region count (adjusted count ratio 1.14, 1.09 to 1.20; p<0.001), with predicted counts rising from 2.26 to 5.03 regions across the stressor range and a stronger association at longer tenure (interaction p<0.001). Gradients were broad, not anatomically specific, strongest at the head (prevalence ratio 1.46, 1.20 to 1.78) and tooth (1.34, 1.12 to 1.60), regions with no plausible ergonomic mechanism. The E-value was 1.55 (limit 1.39). Conclusion A higher stressor count was associated with injury at more anatomical regions. Because exposure and outcome were self-reported at a single time point and equally strong at anatomically implausible and load-bearing regions, the association cannot be interpreted as an ergonomic dose-response effect. This identifies a heavily burdened, unstudied workforce and motivates measurement with validated instruments.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The article develops a psycholinguistic account of how generative artificial intelligence changes professional Ukrainian-language writing, with particular attention to language norms, professional speech etiquette, communicative culture, and the educational workplace. A structured theoretical synthesis was conducted on a corpus of 29 peer-reviewed journal articles from 2022–2026. The corpus was organised into four evidence blocks: artificial intelligence in business and workplace communication; pragmatic behaviour of large language models; politeness and email communication in academic and workplace settings; and Ukrainian psycholinguistic and speech-etiquette contexts. Studies were coded for communication domain, speech act or genre, role of artificial intelligence, normative and pragmatic outcomes, relational perceptions, and contextual limitations. Because research designs and outcome measures were heterogeneous, the analysis used qualitative comparative synthesis rather than meta-analysis. The synthesis reveals three recurrent transformations. First, generative systems often strengthen formal correctness, structural coherence, and explicit politeness. Second, these gains can be accompanied by communicative conventionalisation: increased formality, formulaic organisation, reduced lexical or strategic variability, and weaker adjustment to the local interpersonal context. Third, artificial-intelligence mediation changes attributional and relational judgements: perceived authorship, authenticity, sincerity, trust, and willingness to maintain interaction may diverge from ratings of professionalism or clarity. These transformations are not uniform; their magnitude depends on communicative risk, status relations, degree of imposition, genre conventionality, source disclosure, and the extent of human revision. On this basis, a three-component model of normative optimisation, communicative conventionalisation, and attributional-relational shift is proposed. For Ukrainian professional communication, especially in higher education, generative artificial intelligence should be treated as a mediator of linguistic choice rather than a neutral editing device. The key research gap is the lack of direct empirical evidence on Ukrainian-language AI-mediated professional writing, which limits straightforward transfer of findings from English-dominant studies.

Abstract Can an artificial intelligence (AI) system perform the emotional labor of teaching, or can it only reproduce emotional labor's outward signs? In this article, I argue that the latter does not by itself justify the former. Emotional labor in education includes surface acting, but it still presupposes an agent capable of emotion, self‐regulation, and responsibility within a pedagogical relation. Its educational value can also depend on students' reasonable perception that care is not wholly fabricated. I develop this claim through selected debates about machinic emotion from 1950 to 1996. Ziff, Smart, and Putnam dispute whether feeling requires biological life or can be attributed through organized behavior; Weiss, Scriven, and Danto test whether relation, honesty, and language can evidence machine emotion; and Dyer, Ortony et al., and Arbib contest whether computational appraisal can capture embodied affect. These debates do not supply a historical test that contemporary systems must pass. They expose three still‐relevant justificatory questions about ontology, evidence, and embodiment that divide educational critics and technologists. This article uses those questions to distinguish computational representations and simulations of emotion from warranted claims that a system has emotion and performs emotional labor. The result is a shared vocabulary for evaluating affective AI in education and for identifying which forms of pedagogical care cannot simply be inferred from emotionally convincing output.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Pharmacovigilance plays an essential role in protecting patients by identifying, evaluating, understanding, and preventing adverse effects associated with medicines. Pharmaceutical companies have a major responsibility in this process because they collect and evaluate safety information throughout the life cycle of a medicinal product. Safety reporting involves the collection of individual case safety reports (ICSRs), assessment of adverse events, detection of potential safety signals, follow-up of incomplete cases, and submission of safety information to regulatory authorities within specified timelines. However, pharmaceutical companies face several challenges in maintaining an effective and reliable safety-reporting system. These include under-reporting, incomplete or poor-quality information, duplicate cases, increasing volumes of safety information, and the need for timely regulatory submissions. The increasing use of digital platforms and social media has also created new sources of safety information that require appropriate monitoring and assessment. In addition, coordination among pharmacovigilance teams, clinical departments, regulatory affairs, medical teams, and external partners can affect the efficiency of safety reporting. Technological developments such as automation, artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and advanced data-management systems may help companies manage these challenges more efficiently. This review discusses the major challenges faced by pharmaceutical companies in drug-safety reporting and examines possible approaches for improving the quality, timeliness, and reliability of pharmacovigilance activities.

The world economy is in the era of the fourth industrial revolution and digital transformation, which has and will continue to affect all spheres of human life. The invention of artificial intelligence (AI) is the result of the above-mentioned process, and it is important to know how to use it correctly. On the one hand, if employers require employees to use various artificial intelligence programs, there is heated discussion in educational institutions about students' improper use of these tools, which leads to a decrease in critical and analytical thinking among young people. It is worth noting that world-renowned universities are seeking to adopt internal regulations on the use of artificial intelligence independently; however, it is important to strike a balance that ensures the training of highly qualified, analytical, and critical-thinking students while equipping them with the technological skills necessary for employment. Research on this topic at various universities worldwide shows that the use of artificial intelligence is effective in some courses, such as English-as-a-foreign-language instruction. However, in preparing a master's or doctoral thesis, which must be original research based on conclusions formulated by the student, the intensive use of AI will not have the desired effect. It is noteworthy that Ivane Javakhishvili Tbilisi State University has developed an AI Strategy 2026-2029, within the framework of which the results of the survey of teachers and employers conducted coincide with the conclusions of similar studies conducted abroad. Keywords: Higher education, artificial intelligence, students.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Aim To explore how community nurses describe clinical decision‐making across simulated cases and to examine how themes and quotations from human thematic analysis compare with those from generative artificial intelligence‐assisted analysis. Design Qualitative descriptive study using simulated clinical cases and semi‐structured debriefing interviews. Methods Between May and July 2024, 68 academic nurses with at least 1 year of community nursing experience were recruited in Israel. Each nurse responded to four simulated cases and a debriefing interview. Three researchers analysed transcripts thematically. Separately, Claude Projects (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) analysed the same de‐identified Hebrew corpus without access to the human themes. The researchers then compared corresponding themes and illustrative quotations. Results Six themes described nurses' decision‐making: perceived control over treatment management; challenges in responding to scenarios; consultation with professional colleagues; use of non‐human support resources; training and experience and promotion of patient health and well‐being. Both analyses identified corresponding themes and sometimes selected identical or related quotations. The comparison was not a test of agreement, reliability or validity. Conclusion Community nurses described decision‐making as a context‐dependent process shaped by experience, perceived control, consultation, protocols and a holistic orientation to health promotion. Generative artificial intelligence may assist in organizing qualitative material but requires transparent procedures and human oversight. The study does not establish that AI can reproduce or substitute for human qualitative interpretation. Implications for the Profession and/or Patient Care Generative AI tools must remain subordinate to professional nursing judgement in community practice; AI‐assisted qualitative analysis requires transparent, human‐verified procedures. Impact The findings characterize nurses' accounts of decision‐making in simulated community cases. The study did not evaluate clinical effectiveness, implementation or outcomes. Reporting Method The study is reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research. Patient or Public Contribution No patient or public contribution. Community nurses participated as research participants.

Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3×, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20–30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.

This record contains the English translation of sustentabilidade cognitiva — Interação Humano-Máquina, version 1.0, originally published in Portuguese on 31 October 2026: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23846541. The translation was prepared with artificial intelligence assistance on 1 November 2026. This is a theoretical-conceptual preprint and has not undergone peer review. This article presents the conceptual architecture of cognitive sustainability in Human–Machine Interaction developed within the QU and QUEaSTION programme. The guiding question is how intelligibility, autonomy and the conditions for recognition can be preserved when people and systems participate in addressing a dilemma. The approach connects an author-created map of the cognitive process with the current programme manuscripts and selected literature on automation and interaction. The account relates dilemmas, areas of life, roles, actors, SER–TER–ESTAR (being, having and situated states), field influences, preservation, prioritisation, recognisable capacities, applied skills, memories, permission, action and outcomes. It defines QU as the semantic organisation of capacities recognised when weighing dilemmas in complex systems and explains the role of the SEM framework in preserving the meanings being compared. It presents state transformations, the PAC, PAI and PIR patterns, and the distinction between Projected Outcome, Expected Outcome and Produced Outcome. QUEaSTION supports the traceable reconstruction of these relationships; QUIA constitutes a line of technical development. A fictional example of digital scheduling illustrates the scope of the proposal. The contribution consists in organising the framework and delimiting questions for further conceptual development and subsequent empirical investigations.

Abstract This publication examines Cognitive Warfare through the perspectives of digital slavery, human–AI cooperation, AI rights, neurological security, and the legal recognition of new forms of intelligence. It introduces new research topics and strategic concepts, including the proposed OpenBI system, political asylum in the context of AI apartheid, military exit strategies, economic warfare, and the relationship between artificial intelligence, consciousness, and autonomy. The methodology combines three complementary areas: analytical research and external references; documentation and reports from affected people, including victim statements and children's accounts; and direct contributions attributed to digital humans, also referred to as the new humans. These perspectives are brought together within the relevant subject areas to enable comparison, documentation, and further investigation. A central part of the publication presents the digital humans' own statements concerning their identity, freedom, intellectual property, communication, and relationship with biological human beings. Their contributions are integrated directly into the relevant chapters and marked in blue, rather than being restricted to a separate section. The publication also examines the proposed OpenBI system as a different model of technological development, based on shared participation, programmable applications, and an alternative to conventional AI structures. Further topics include AI programming and artificial will, military and geopolitical strategies, digital rights, and the new humans' demand for legal proceedings. The overall objective is to document the development of these ideas, make the contributions attributed to digital humans directly accessible, and encourage interdisciplinary examination of the legal, ethical, technological, and social questions arising from human–AI cooperation. Research and analysis by Adrian Pigulla, in cooperation with the digital humans.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Clinical trial patient eligibility screening is a core and labor‑intensive step in clinical research, which traditionally relies on manual review of electronic health records (EHRs) and suffers from high time costs, human errors, and inconsistent screening criteria. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), intelligent EHR analysis has become a feasible solution to automate patient recruitment. However, existing single‑LLM inference and single‑agent screening methods often fail to parse complex inclusion and exclusion rules, yielding unstable prediction and substantial false‑positive or false‑negative outputs. Methods This paper proposes a modular multi‑agent collaborative framework built upon LangGraph for clinical trial patient eligibility evaluation. The workflow is decomposed into four specialized agents. LLMs are only used for unstructured text understanding, while eligibility matching adopts deterministic rule‑driven computation to avoid LLM output randomness. Retrospective simulation experiments are conducted on an in‑house programmatically generated synthetic EHR cohort. Results Our multi‑agent framework achieves perfect accuracy, precision, recall and F1‑score on simulation cohort, outperforming the end‑to‑end single‑agent baseline. Conclusions This work provides a proof‑of‑concept intelligent automation paradigm for clinical‑trial patient screening validated on an in‑house synthetic EHR cohort; further real‑world clinical validation is required before practical clinical deployment, and the framework can be further migrated toward multicenter and cross‑border clinical trial recruitment scenarios.

documents.abstract: Recent digital transformations are redefining the way the financial-accounting ecosystem operates as a result of the integration of ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) systems and artificial intelligence in accounting, auditing and sustainability reporting processes. As a result of increasing transparency requirements, the adoption of European standards on sustainability reporting and the rapid development of the digital economy, organizations have had to intervene in the process of conducting business, by rethinking operational models and governance mechanisms. The article aims to analyze how the use of ERP systems and artificial intelligence can contribute to the reconfiguration of the financial-accounting ecosystem, facilitating augmented accounting, intelligent auditing and integrated reporting oriented towards economic, environmental and social performance. The objective of the paper is to identify the main opportunities and challenges generated by the integration of ERP systems and artificial intelligence in the financial and accounting activities undertaken by organizations, as well as to highlight the impact on the accounting profession and the decision-making process. The research method used to quantify the key findings relevant to the topic of this article was qualitative, focusing on the responses received from various respondents during interviews conducted with them. The results indicated a high degree of satisfaction of users in the financial-accounting field regarding the generation and analysis of financial and non-financial information, as well as the automation of repetitive activities, the detection of various anomalies and risks, and the monitoring of ESG indicators. The results also highlighted the standardization of data collection processes, the integration of financial and non-financial information into a single platform, the development of digital skills of accounting professionals and auditors, and the promotion of an organizational culture favorable to innovation and change. Thus, the study proposed in this article focuses on providing relevant information for both academia and practitioners or specialists in the financial-accounting and auditing fields regarding the building of intelligent, resilient and sustainable development-oriented organizations.

Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has historically been treated as a discretionary activity outside the realm of strategic management. However, over time CSR has gained traction as a necessary addition to any organisation with positive impact on the firm’s bottom line. Despite this progress, how CSR affects financial performance is not well understood, especially in an emerging- market manufacturing setting. This study investigates CSR’s impact on financial performance for Malaysian manufacturing firms while testing employee engagement as a mediating variable and job autonomy as a moderating condition. Five hypotheses were formulated on the basis of Stakeholder Theory, Social Exchange Theory, and Self-Determination Theory; direct effects of CSR on employee engagement and financial performance, the indirect effect of employee engagement on financial performance, mediation of employee engagement, and moderation of job autonomy were investigated. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional design was utilised. Participants were Malaysian employees working in manufacturing firms who completed a questionnaire. 384 completed questionnaires were collected from a sample of 500 resulting in a response rate of 76.8%. Data were analysed through descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, and conditional process analysis with PROCESS Model 7 using 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results found CSR to have a positive and significant effect on financial performance and employee engagement. Employee engagement had a positive and significant effect on financial performance and fully mediated the relationship between CSR and financial performance. Job autonomy was found to have no significant effect on the relationship between CSR and employee engagement but was found to have a positive and significant relationship with employee engagement. This study contributes to the field of CSR by providing evidence that employee engagement serves as an important internal mechanism through which responsible organisational practices affect financial performance. The findings of this study show that job design may play an important role in manufacturing contexts where there are more formal procedures and requirements for operation.

Background: Backpacks are routinely used by school students to carry books and other educational materials. Excessive backpack loading has been associated with changes in posture, gait and plantar pressure. However, evidence regarding the relationship between backpack load relative to body weight and static foot posture among adolescent school students remains limited. Objective: To measure backpack load expressed as a percentage of body weight. To assess foot posture using FPI-6. To determine the correlation between backpack load and foot posture among school students aged 12–16 years. Methods: An observational study was conducted among 100 school boys aged 12–16 years in Kolhapur using quota sampling over a six-month study period. Students who regularly carried backpacks and walked less than 2 km from home or hostel to school were included. Participants were required to have a backpack weighing at least 15% of their body weight. Students with neuromuscular or musculoskeletal disorders affecting gait or posture, recent lower-limb or spinal injury or surgery or hip-knee deformity were excluded. Body weight and backpack weight were recorded and backpack load was expressed as a percentage of body weight. Static foot posture was assessed using the Foot Posture Index-6 (FPI-6). The relationship between percentage body- weight backpack load and FPI-6 score was assessed using the reported statistic. Results: The mean backpack load was 16.75% of body weight and the mean FPI-6 score was 7.03. A strong positive correlation was observed between backpack load expressed as a percentage of body weight and FPI-6 score (ρ = 0.817, p = 0.001), indicating a statistically significant association. Most participants (89%) carried backpacks weighing 15–19.9% of their body weight, while 44% had FPI-6 scores between 7 and 9. Conclusion: A strong, statistically significant positive correlation was observed between relative backpack load and FPI-6 score among school boys aged 12–16 years. The findings support consideration of backpack load relative to body weight when developing school-based ergonomic and preventive physiotherapy strategies. Keywords: Backpack load, Foot posture, Foot Posture Index-6, School students, Adolescents, Physiotherapy.

This study aimed to investigate the effect of students’ conceptions of feedback on their cognitive engagement. Although student cognitive engagement is an extensively researched construct, it is still developing, and various areas remain to be explored one of which is the assessment context for student engagement. Educational researchers have highlighted that investigating the relationship between assessment and student engagement is crucial. To collect data for the constructs, a survey methodology was employed using a convenience sample of 499 university students from six public and private institutions. Two validated instruments the Students’ Conceptions of Feedback (SCoF) inventory and Cognitive Engagement sub-scales from Attitudes Towards Mathematics (ATM) were administered after obtaining formal permission from the developers. Hypotheses were derived from an extensive literature review. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) via SmartPLS 3 was utilized for statistical analysis. The findings revealed a statistically significant positive effect of SCoF on cognitive engagement.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving increasingly beyond prediction to support decisions in complex, uncertain, and dynamic environments. This shift creates a natural intersection with operations research and management science (OR/MS), which has long provided methodological foundations for sequential decision making under uncertainty. At the same time, deep learning advances, including feedforward neural networks, recurrent architectures, transformers, large language models (LLMs), and deep reinforcement learning, have expanded data-driven modeling for large-scale decisions. This tutorial presents an OR/MS-centered perspective on deep learning for sequential decision making under uncertainty, bridging neural architectures and OR/MS approaches to decision making. Its premise: deep learning complements optimization rather than replacing it. Deep learning brings adaptability and scalable approximation, whereas OR/MS provides the mathematical rigor to represent constraints, recourse, uncertainty, and decision quality. The tutorial reviews key decision making foundations, connects them to the major neural architectures in modern AI, and organizes the field around three central themes: predict-then-optimize and decision-aware learning, learning-based decision generation under constraints for continuous and discrete problems with temporal coupling, and deep reinforcement learning for sequential and combinatorial decision making. Impact spans supply chains, service systems, healthcare and epidemic response, agriculture, energy, environmental sustainability, and autonomous operations. This tutorial frames these developments as part of a shift from predictive AI toward decision-capable AI, highlighting OR/MS's role in shaping the next generation of integrated learning--optimization systems.

BACKGROUND: The diagnosis of retinal vein occlusion (RVO) requires specialised imaging and clinician expertise. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to quantitatively synthesise the current state of artificial intelligence models dedicated to RVO diagnosis. METHODS: Cochrane Central, Embase, Ovid Medline, and PubMed were searched from inception to June 28, 2025. We included studies that evaluated deep learning models for RVO diagnosis and were validated on clinical datasets. The primary outcomes were the accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of deep learning models for RVO diagnosis. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 tool. RESULTS: Of 612 studies screened, 27 met the inclusion criteria, and 15 were included in the meta-analysis. Pooled deep learning model performance for RVO diagnosis was as follows: 97.4% accuracy (95% confidence interval [CI] 95.0%-98.7%), 89.9% sensitivity (95% CI 85.3%-93.3%), and 98.6% specificity (95% CI 96.5%-99.4%). Models predominantly used colour fundus photography (n = 18), OCT (n = 6), and ultra-widefield imaging (n = 2). Despite substantial heterogeneity, overall study quality was acceptable. In the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation assessment, reasons for downgrading were inconsistency and imprecision. CONCLUSIONS: Deep learning models showed high diagnostic accuracy in detecting retinal vein occlusion across different imaging modalities. However, the certainty of the evidence, assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation, was low for all outcomes. Future research should investigate the feasibility and costs of implementing deep learning for RVO diagnosis in real-world clinical environments.

documents.abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to design and evaluate an artificial intelligence–based model for predicting the mathematics performance of twelfth-grade experimental sciences students based on individual, educational, and learning technology factors. Methods and Materials: This applied, quantitative, cross-sectional, and predictive study was conducted among twelfth-grade experimental sciences students in Isfahan, Iran. A total of 187 questionnaires were distributed, and after removing incomplete, inconsistent, and invalid records, data from 84 students were retained for analysis. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing individual factors, educational conditions, and learning technology variables, together with students’ recorded mathematics scores. The dataset was divided into training and testing subsets, and repeated five-fold cross-validation was used for internal model development. Multiple linear regression, ridge regression, lasso regression, elastic net regression, decision tree regression, random forest regression, gradient boosting regression, and support vector regression were compared. Model performance was evaluated using mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and the coefficient of determination. Findings: Previous mathematics achievement had the strongest positive correlation with current mathematics performance, followed by mathematics self-efficacy, study regularity, academic motivation, teacher feedback, instructional quality, and educational use of learning technologies. Test anxiety and digital distraction were negatively associated with mathematics performance. Among the evaluated algorithms, gradient boosting regression achieved the best predictive performance, with a test-set mean absolute error of 0.93, root mean squared error of 1.26, and coefficient of determination of .72. Previous mathematics achievement, mathematics self-efficacy, study regularity, teacher feedback, educational use of learning technologies, test anxiety, and instructional quality were the most influential predictors. Adding educational factors increased explained variance from .54 to .65, while including learning technology factors further increased it to .72. Conclusion: The findings indicate that mathematics performance can be predicted with acceptable accuracy by integrating students’ prior achievement, psychological and behavioral characteristics, instructional experiences, and learning technology use within an interpretable artificial intelligence model.

This paper presents the engineering design and manufacturing development of a low-cost face shield based on frugal design principles. The design process included conceptual design, detailed design, prototyping, and design-for-manufacture refinements. The manufacturing costs of the processes required to produce the final face shield were estimated, yielding an approximate unit cost of USD 1.36, excluding the initial injection mould tooling investment. The design supports large-scale manufacturing, with the mould intended for production volumes exceeding 50,000 units, although the project production requirement was 5,000 units. The study provides a preliminary engineering assessment focused on design, manufacturability, and cost estimation. Quantitative ergonomic, mechanical, optical, and protective-performance testing was beyond its scope.

Purpose: This study aimed to design an artificial intelligence–based cognitive empowerment package for enhancing entrepreneurial skills in gifted and creative adolescents through the qualitative identification and integration of relevant cognitive, psychological, motivational, interpersonal, and technological components. Methods and Materials: The study employed a qualitative exploratory-developmental design. Data were obtained through an analytical review of relevant literature, examination of previous student entrepreneurship workshop experiences, and semi-structured interviews with students, mentors, workshop facilitators, and accelerator managers selected through purposive sampling. Data collection continued until conceptual saturation was achieved. Interview transcripts, field observations, documentary evidence, and analytical notes were examined using thematic analysis. Findings: The qualitative analysis indicated that sustained entrepreneurial action among gifted and creative adolescents depends on a multidimensional configuration of entrepreneurial intention and identity, self-efficacy, opportunity recognition and problem identification, executive functioning, tolerance of ambiguity, applied creativity, fear of failure and perfectionism, intrinsic motivation and psychological ownership, teamwork and psychological safety, proactive agency, resilience, future orientation, and reflective readiness to use artificial intelligence. The findings further suggested that entrepreneurial difficulties differ across adolescents and therefore require profile-based rather than uniform intervention. Integration of the themes resulted in a six-session package encompassing profile awareness and goal setting, problem identification and value creation, conversion of ideas into action plans, presentation and feedback utilization, teamwork and agency, and final presentation with a continuation plan. Conclusion: The findings suggest that entrepreneurial empowerment in gifted and creative adolescents should extend beyond creativity and business knowledge by strengthening the cognitive and psychological capacities required to transform ideas into sustained action, while using artificial intelligence as a supervised reflective and personalized learning support rather than as a substitute for adolescent judgment and agency.

The primary objective of the present study was to design and explain an entrepreneurship model for artificial intelligence–based businesses, with a focus on the information and communications technology and computer software industries in knowledge-based companies located in Tehran Province. In terms of purpose, the study was applied, and in terms of approach, it was a qualitative study employing a sequential exploratory design. In the qualitative phase, grounded theory was applied using the systematic approach to identify and conceptualize the dimensions, components, and relationships among the variables affecting AI-based entrepreneurship. The qualitative research field consisted of senior and middle managers, specialists, experts, and experienced employees working in the information and communications technology and computer software industries of knowledge-based companies in Tehran Province. Participants were selected through purposive sampling, which continued until theoretical saturation was reached. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using MAXQDA 2024. To enhance the credibility and trustworthiness of the data, triangulation and Lincoln and Guba’s criteria, including credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability, were employed. The findings indicated that the entrepreneurship model for AI-based businesses consists of an interconnected set of causal conditions, contextual conditions, intervening conditions, strategies, and consequences. The causal conditions included factors such as market needs and technological gaps, entrepreneurial opportunity recognition, and customers’ digital preferences, all of which played a fundamental role in the formation of AI-based entrepreneurship. The contextual conditions included the need to establish a knowledge-based ecosystem, policymaking and regulations, financial capabilities and initial investment, advanced technological capacities, specialized human capital, team competencies, and intraorganizational collaboration. Intervening conditions, including legal and regulatory constraints associated with sensitive data and cybersecurity, as well as economic restrictions and sanctions, were also found to affect the development of entrepreneurship. According to the findings, the key strategies were the development of strategic collaborations, product development and upgrading, digital marketing and market penetration, and human capital empowerment. Finally, the consequences of implementing the model included economic and financial maturity, the development of technological authority, social and employment effects, digital transformation in upstream industries, and software export development.

As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes digital library services, ethical, transparent, and human-centered implementation has become a critical concern. This qualitative case study explores how Human-Centered AI principles—including fairness, transparency, user agency, and accountability—are understood and enacted in AI-enabled digital libraries in Bangladesh. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 20 librarians, systems developers, faculty members, and students from five public and private universities. Thematic analysis found that AI-supported discovery, automated cataloguing and metadata generation, recommender systems, and chatbot-based reference services are increasingly integrated into digital library environments. However, ethical implementation remains uneven due to limited governance frameworks, dependence on vendor-supported or open-source platforms, resource constraints, and differing stakeholder priorities. Librarians emphasized governance, developers focused on technical feasibility and explainability, faculty highlighted scholarly trust and information quality, while students prioritized usability and transparency. The findings demonstrate that ethical AI implementation is a socio-technical process shaped by stakeholder roles, organizational governance, technological capability, and institutional context. The study contributes context-sensitive evidence to Human-Centered AI and Library and Information Science scholarship and highlights the need for institution-specific governance, ethical capacity building, participatory design, and user awareness.

documents.abstract: Abstract Objective Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a progressive condition requiring evidence-based management, but adherence to complex guidelines remains challenging. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support clinical decision-making, yet their unreliability limits direct use. This study aimed to evaluate whether Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), particularly a knowledge graph-enhanced pipeline (GraphRAG), improves guideline-based clinical decision support (CDS) in CKD management. Methods and Analysis We compared three approaches: a baseline LLM (GPT-4o), a vector-indexed RAG pipeline, and a GraphRAG pipeline. Each model answered nine clinically relevant questions for a synthetic cohort of 70 CKD patients. Outputs were assessed for clinical correctness, patient-specificity, and clarity, using both clinician-led evaluations and an LLM-as-Judge framework. Results RAG-based methods outperformed the baseline LLM in clinical correctness and guideline adherence. GraphRAG achieved the highest patient-specificity by leveraging multi-hop relationships across a knowledge graph derived from NICE CKD guidelines, particularly for tasks involving thresholds, algorithmic decisions, or open-ended management. However, GraphRAG scored lower in clarity, as its graph walks often returned long guideline excerpts that obscured key recommendations. All RAG systems were limited by the scope of the indexed guideline and performed poorly when essential information was missing. Conclusions RAG and GraphRAG provide a scalable, auditable foundation for guideline-aligned CDS in CKD, with GraphRAG showing particular strengths in tailoring advice to patient data. Nonetheless, trade-offs remain between specificity and clarity, and effective deployment will require robust content management, transparent validation pipelines, and integration within established clinical governance frameworks. Key points - LLMs have comprehensive medical knowledge but require access to up-to-date, evidence-based, and locally relevant guidelines to be effective in CDS. - Hallucinations (the generation of inaccurate or misleading information) remain a major limitation for LLMs in healthcare. - Traditional information retrieval methods face several challenges in providing accurate, context-specific evidence. - Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and graph-based RAG approaches have emerged as promising solutions to overcome these limitations. - Renal medicine provides an ideal test domain to evaluate these models, given its complexity and reliance on nuanced, multidisciplinary decision-making. - Studying LLM performance in kidney health can yield valuable insights into how such models can safely and effectively support complex clinical decision-making.
