documents.abstract: Abstract This study aimed to develop and validate a practical nomogram to screen poor sleep quality among night-shift nurses, providing an effective screening tool for managing their occupational health. A cross-sectional study was conducted involving 595 night-shift nurses selected between January and March 2026. The nurses were randomly divided into two groups in a ratio of 7:3. Data were collected using a general information questionnaire, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, the Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale, and the Fatigue scale-14. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were conducted to develop a nomogram model. The performance was evaluated by discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. The nomogram included eight associated factors: age, marital status, department affiliation, weekly working hours, monthly night shifts, drinking coffee or tea, generalized anxiety disorder, and fatigue. The area under the ROC curve in the training and validation set was 0.856 (95% CI: 0.823–0.882) and 0.849 (95% CI: 0.821–0.876), respectively. Calibration showed excellent fit across all datasets. The decision curve confirmed that the nomogram offers good clinical net benefits. This study provides a simple and practical tool for occupational health screening, early intervention, and targeted health management in medical institutions.

Abstract Background In this study, we aimed to develop and evaluate an artificial intelligence-based diagnostic model for the diagnosis of acute cholecystitis (AC) using non-contrast CT images and clinical data. Methods This retrospective study included 197 patients (100 AC, 97 non-AC) treated between January 2016 and December 2025 at a single center. Patients were randomly divided into training (n = 139) and test (n = 58) datasets. Three models were constructed: an imaging-based deep learning model, a clinical data-based machine learning model, and a hybrid machine learning model integrating deep learning-derived imaging features with clinical data. CT images were preprocessed, and gallbladder regions were segmented. Clinical variables included white blood cell counts and levels of C-reactive protein and liver function markers. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Statistical comparisons were performed using Welch's t-test and Chi-square test. Results The imaging-based model achieved accuracy 0.741, precision 0.703, recall 0.867, specificity 0.607, F1 score 0.776, and AUC 0.863. The blood-based model achieved accuracy 0.914, precision 0.931, recall 0.900, specificity 0.929, F1 score 0.915, and AUC 0.946. The hybrid model showed the highest performance, with accuracy 0.931, precision 0.882, recall 1.000, specificity 0.857, F1 score 0.938, and AUC 0.996. Conclusions A hybrid model integrating CT imaging and clinical data improved diagnostic performance for AC compared with single-modality models.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: This study focused on developing a Dual-Function Ergonomically Smart Settee (D-FESS) tailored for academic offices in the Faculty of Technology, University of Ibadan, Nigeria. The goal was to optimize office space use and support casual, intermittent rest to reduce stress among academic staff. A preliminary survey was conducted from November 2023 to March 2024, involving 33 purposively selected academic staff. Data were gathered using structured questionnaires, oral interviews, direct office assessments and anthropometric measurements. Results showed that academics spend 5 to 16 hours daily in their offices, with about 70% of this time seated, indicating a sedentary work pattern. A majority (96%) reported experiencing work-related stress and expressed a need for a D-FESS. Average office space was 4.5 m by 4.3 m, with some unused space available for new furniture. Anthropometric data were collected and the 95th percentile values were used to design and fabricate a D-FESS suitable for one academic office. The study established the need for ergonomic, space-efficient furniture like D-FESS to enhance comfort and productivity in academic environments.

The rapid development of digital technologies is transforming modern economies by creating new mechanisms of production, distribution, consumption, and public administration. This article examines the theoretical foundations and current trends of the digital economy, focusing on the experience of the Republic of Uzbekistan. Particular attention is given to the "Digital Uzbekistan – 2030" strategy, digital infrastructure, e-government, digital finance, e-commerce, the IT sector, and human capital development. The study applies systematic, comparative, and institutional approaches, as well as the analysis of statistical and regulatory information. The findings show that Uzbekistan has established important institutional and technological foundations for digital transformation. However, challenges remain, including the digital divide, a shortage of qualified specialists, cybersecurity risks, unequal regional access to digital infrastructure, and regulatory gaps. The study proposes strengthening digital infrastructure, developing digital skills, expanding the application of artificial intelligence and big data, supporting digital entrepreneurship, and promoting international digital integration. RU Стремительное развитие цифровых технологий трансформирует современные экономики посредством формирования новых механизмов производства, распределения, потребления и государственного управления. В статье рассматриваются теоретические основы и современные тенденции развития цифровой экономики с акцентом на опыт Республики Узбекистан. Особое внимание уделяется стратегии «Цифровой Узбекистан – 2030», цифровой инфраструктуре, электронному правительству, цифровым финансам, электронной коммерции, IT-сектору и развитию человеческого капитала. В исследовании применяются системный, сравнительный и институциональный подходы, а также анализ статистической и нормативно-правовой информации. This article examines the didactic potential and limitations of generative artificial intelligence in teaching Russian as a foreign language. Its aim is to classify instructional scenarios and identify conditions for pedagogically appropriate implementation. The materials include scholarly and methodological publications, UNESCO guidance, and illustrative activities designed to develop grammatical, lexical, and communicative competence. The study employs literature analysis, comparison of teaching approaches, and qualitative evaluation of learning situations. Discussed applications include exercises on case government and verb forms, simulated dialogues, preliminary feedback on written responses, and support for independent practice. Potential limitations include inaccurate explanations, stylistically inappropriate suggestions, insufficient sensitivity to cultural context, and reduced learner autonomy. The article proposes a six stage instructional sequence: independent task completion, artificial intelligence assistance, critical checking, teacher feedback, revision, and renewed independent performance. It also emphasizes personal data protection and expert review of automatically generated recommendations. The research is theoretical and methodological; no classroom experiment or measured learning outcomes are reported. The framework combines digital assistance, teacher guidance, and independent practice. Future classroom validation remains necessary.

The rapid expansion of the digital economy is transforming global production and consumption systems, yet its environmental implications remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the relationship between the Digital Economy Index (DEI) and ecological footprint (EF) across 77 developed and developing countries from 2001 to 2020. An integrated empirical framework combining fixed-effects and System GMM estimation with machine learning techniques, Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machine (SVM), is employed to provide complementary econometric and predictive evidence. Econometric results show that digitalization significantly reduces EF on average, with stronger environmental benefits observed in developed economies. Moderation analysis reveals that industrialization and trade openness weaken these environmental benefits, whereas artificial intelligence, ICT development, and renewable energy transitions strengthen them. The transmission-channel analysis further suggests that environmental technological innovation and changes in the energy structure may represent potential pathways linking digitalization to environmental outcomes. The machine learning analysis provides complementary predictive evidence and identifies a nonlinear pattern in the DEI–EF relationship, potentially exhibiting an inverted U-shape in which ecological pressure increases at earlier stages of digitalization but declines at more advanced stages. RF and SVM achieve predictive accuracies of 94% and 80%, respectively. Overall, the findings indicate that digitalization is not inherently green and that its environmental benefits depend on the stage of digital development and broader structural and technological conditions, highlighting the importance of clean energy integration and sustainable digital transformation.

In a context of demographic ageing and accelerating digital transformation, understanding the impact of digitalisation on older workers is increasingly relevant. This chapter explores how these shifts shape social and health inequalities among older workers in Portugal. Using national and European data, it outlines trends in employment, education, and health for workers aged 55 and over and examines the growing digital divide between generations. It also identifies policy initiatives and best practices that promote digital inclusion and support older adults’ participation in the workforce. Special attention is given to the effects of remote work, digital skills gaps, and workplace ergonomics. The chapter concludes with recommendations for inclusive policies that foster active ageing, reduce disparities, and ensure older workers remain valued in a digital society.

documents.abstract: This article examines the digital transformation of international law as a multidimensional process of rethinking traditional mechanisms of international interaction. It is argued that the penetration of digital technologies into the sphere of international legal regulation leads not only to the emergence of new objects of legal protection but also to the transformation of established approaches to determining state jurisdiction, enforcing international responsibility, and ensuring compliance with international obligations. The paper identifies the key challenges of the digital age for international law, including the fragmentation of international regulation of the digital environment, the asymmetry of states’ technological capabilities, the complexity of establishing liability for cross-border digital offenses, and the need to harmonize cybersecurity requirements with international human rights standards. The study emphasizes that the effectiveness of international legal regulation increasingly depends on the ability of international institutions and states to ensure the interaction of universal legal principles with flexible mechanisms for responding to technological risks without undermining guarantees of human rights, state sovereignty, and international security. Promising directions for legal development are outlined, including the improvement of international standards for digital governance, the formation of coordinated approaches to international legal liability for the use of digital technologies, the strengthening of international cooperation in the field of cybersecurity, and the development of regulatory mechanisms to oversee the use of artificial intelligence. The paper demonstrates the advisability of transitioning from a piecemeal response to individual technological threats to a systematic model of international legal regulation based on the principles of coherence and respect for fundamental human rights. It is concluded that the digital transformation of international law represents not only a technology-driven challenge but also an opportunity to renew its normative potential, institutional capacity, and instruments for ensuring the international legal order in the context of global digital interdependence.

Informal digital learning of English (IDLE) — learners' self-organized engagement with English through short videos, social media, streaming, gaming, and generative AI outside the classroom — has accumulated a large body of empirical research over the past decade, yet its affective and individual-difference correlates have never been quantitatively synthesized. Existing meta-analyses address only overall effects on achievement, and narrative reviews of emotion and individual-difference variables have pooled no effect sizes. This preregistration reports a three-level meta-analysis that (1) estimates the strength of association between IDLE and positive emotions, negative emotions, and individual-difference variables; (2) tests whether the association with positive emotions is stronger than that with negative emotions, as predicted by broaden-and-build and control-value theories; and (3) explores whether the affective pathway is conditional on trait-like individual differences. Ten sources (Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, OpenAlex, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, CNKI, Scopus) will be searched for correlational studies published from 2014 onward. Effect sizes (Pearson's r, Fisher's z-transformed) will be modeled with three-level random-effects models cross-validated by cluster-robust variance estimation, with seven prespecified moderators and publication-bias correction (PET-PEESE). Expected outcomes are the first preregistered, effect-size-level synthesis of the IDLE–affect/individual-difference literature, clarifying whether IDLE works through feelings or through traits.

This is a model draft of an international treaty on artificial intelligence governance. It is not a binding instrument and has not been adopted, signed or ratified by any State. The draft is built around human dignity, human agency and the protection of persons in vulnerable situations; effective human control and an obligation of prior constraint (evaluation of an action before it is generated or takes external effect, with three evaluation "gates" for dignity, ethics and necessity/irreversibility, and a duty to hold and escalate to a human); obligations of developers, providers and deployers; transparency, record-keeping and preservation of evidence; independent audit and technical verification; individual rights to know, to human review, to object and to an effective remedy, with protection of complainants and whistleblowers; and international oversight bodies, cooperation and dispute settlement. The full texts of Annexes I to VII (terms, risk classification and objects of evaluation; the Dignity, Ethics and Necessity Gates; hold, human escalation and record-keeping requirements; the prior constraint mechanism; and independent verification and technical verification standards) are included in draft form and remain subject to the drafting reservations; figures and thresholds are left in square brackets for later determination. The final pages list the drafting reservations and matters requiring legal and technical consideration before any diplomatic negotiation. Comments and suggestions are welcome. The author directed the content, reviewed it, and is responsible for the final text.

documents.abstract: Dynamic PGA: Progressive Boundary Formation extends the Dynamic Personalized Guidance Architecture (Dynamic PGA) framework by examining how personalization, trust, human agency, and boundaries should develop together in adaptive AI experiences. As AI systems become increasingly personalized, usefulness depends not only on what an AI system learns about an individual, but also on understanding what information should not be disclosed, reused, inferred, or carried into another context. This paper introduces Progressive Boundary Formation as a human-centered process through which individuals can recognize, communicate, test, and revise personal, relational, professional, and organizational boundaries as their interaction with AI develops. The framework considers the transition from private AI-assisted exploration to consequential human action, including communication, publication, professional activity, and interactions involving other people. It proposes that boundary awareness should develop alongside personalization and trust rather than appearing only as a static privacy setting or late-stage safeguard. Progressive Boundary Formation is presented as a conceptual extension of Dynamic PGA and its broader goal of creating AI experiences that adapt with the human while preserving human judgment, agency, relationships, and appropriate boundaries. Keywords: Dynamic PGA, Progressive Boundary Formation, artificial intelligence, personalized AI, human-centered AI, adaptive AI, human agency, AI trust, privacy, AI boundaries

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into English language learning through tools that provide adaptive learning, automated feedback, and personalized support. Although previous studies have examined the educational benefits of AI-powered tools, relatively little is known about how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students experience these technologies and how their perspectives can inform the design of learner-centered Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS). This study explored EFL students’ experiences, perceived benefits, challenges, and expectations regarding AI-powered tools for English language learning. A qualitative research design was adopted using semi-structured interviews with nine Vietnamese university EFL students, and the data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that participants experienced AI-powered language learning tools as adaptive, feedback-oriented, and engaging. They particularly valued immediate feedback, flexible learning opportunities, and gamified features, which they associated with greater confidence, motivation, and learner autonomy. At the same time, participants expressed concerns about over-reliance on AI, the contextual and cultural appropriateness of AI-generated feedback, and data privacy and security. Participants also envisioned future ITS as more conversational, personalized, and culturally responsive systems that could better address individual learning needs. Overall, the findings suggest that participants viewed AI as a valuable learning support while emphasizing the importance of independent learning, teacher guidance, and contextual relevance. The study offers preliminary design implications for learner-centered ITS by highlighting the importance of incorporating learners’ experiences and expectations into future AI-supported language learning systems.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Current urban planning treats the subsurface as a passive solid or void, constrained by a “needs to resources” paradigm that marginalizes geological knowledge. Standard mapping methodologies, particularly those using the Analytic Hierarchy Process, rely on manual expert solicitation, which is logistically burdensome and prone to cognitive blind spots. This research proposes a theoretical shift from target-oriented systems to an obstacle-oriented framework. Designating the street segment as the fundamental unit of analysis across the province of Québec, this research presents a prototype that implements a static knowledge-retrieval pipeline where a Large Language Model serves as an informational model for preliminary planning, translating hydrogeological constraints into qualitative assessments. These textual descriptions are then encoded into a continuous partition spectrum using a one-dimensional self-organizing map. The prototype demonstrates high computational robustness in standardizing qualitative data, successfully mapping the geological dichotomy between the stable crystalline basement of the Canadian Shield and the conflict-prone sedimentary basins of the St. Lawrence Lowlands. By converting qualitative data into relational contextual numbers, the model identifies latent synergies without predefined target functions. The article concludes that this pre-specific modeling approach validates the utility of artificial intelligence in mitigating cognitive blind spots, demonstrating how computational models can complement human engineering by repositioning geological insights at the very beginning of the urban design process. By establishing a topos of communication capable of circulating around the inherent opacity of the geological volume, this method offers a scalable instrument for sustainable underground urbanism that treats the earth not as an anecdotal resource, but as an active constituent of the built environment.

The digital transformation has reshaped entrepreneurship, with the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) as a powerful enabler of innovation and startup creation. However, higher education institutions face challenges integrating AI into entrepreneurship education curriculum, limiting students’ ability to fully harness its potential. This study aimed to determine and explore entrepreneurship students’ challenges in using AI for startup development, assess the competencies they gain in innovating business ideas, and analyze how these challenges affect competencies using structural equation modeling (SEM). Employing an convergent mixed-method design, the study surveyed 114 third- and fourth-year BS Entrepreneurship students and conducted interviews to faculty and business plan implementers. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and SEM, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis for triangulation. Findings revealed that students face significant challenges in opportunity identification, decision-making, performance execution, education and learning, and research application. The key barriers highlight was market understanding, lack of AI literacy, limited mentorship, and insufficient curriculum integration. Despite these, students reported gaining competencies in opportunity recognition, customer targeting, data-informed decision-making, and entrepreneurial communication using AI tools. However, critical thinking, problem-solving, and prototyping skills remained underdeveloped. SEM results indicated that challenges in education, opportunity identification, and decision-making significantly constrained entrepreneurial competencies. The study implies the need for higher education to reform curricula by embedding AI-focused modules, case-based projects, mentorship opportunities, and innovation hubs. Strengthening AI-driven entrepreneurship education will equip students with the competencies required for sustainable startup creation in the digital economy.

Abstract Background Clinical reasoning for unstructured problems—those lacking clearly defined initial conditions, standard protocols, or singular correct solutions—remains a persistent challenge in medical education. While artificial intelligence (AI) tools have shown promise in structured knowledge tasks, their integration into frameworks designed for unstructured clinical reasoning remains underexplored. Methods A systems thinking assessment framework was adapted for medical education and validated through expert review and inter-rater reliability testing (ICC = 0.801, 95% CI: 0.725–0.866). Fifty-five medical students were randomly assigned to three groups: an AI-assisted learning group (AIL, n = 18) using ChatGPT 4.0 as a guided reasoning aid, a conventional learning group (CL, n = 18) using textbooks and non-AI online resources, and a manual group (MG, n = 19) without any supplementary tools. All participants responded to the same unstructured clinical case comprising seven tasks (Q1–Q7), each scored on a 0–3 scale by five blinded raters. As an exploratory benchmark, ChatGPT 4.0 responses to the identical case were independently scored using the same framework to characterize the AI model's performance profile and limitations. Results The AIL group achieved the highest mean total score (12.11 ± 1.78), significantly outperforming the CL group (8.94 ± 1.08, p < 0.0001) and the MG (9.97 ± 2.37, p < 0.01). Significant advantages were observed in Q2 (information needs), Q5 (scenario development), Q6 (challenges), and Q7 (unintended consequences). Subgroup analysis revealed no significant interaction between learning tools and baseline academic performance (F = 0.213, p = 0.930, η² = 0.018), suggesting consistent benefits across GPA levels. The ChatGPT 4.0 benchmark produced uniformly identical scores (total score 16.5 across all trials), revealing characteristic limitations in response variability and template dependency. Conclusions An AI-assisted learning framework grounded in a validated systems thinking assessment tool can enhance medical students' clinical reasoning for unstructured problems, with effects that appear independent of baseline academic performance. The ChatGPT benchmark highlights both the capabilities and the rigidities of current AI models, underscoring the need for hybrid human–AI collaboration rather than AI substitution in clinical reasoning education. documents.abstract: The Indonesian startup ecosystem has experienced growing funding pressures and rising demands for operational efficiency, making business sustainability an increasingly important priority. Therefore, this study aims to examine the effect of entrepreneurial orientation on business sustainability, with the quality of Artificial Intelligence (AI) utilization serving as a mediator among startup employees in Greater Jakarta and Bandung. Using a causal quantitative design, the study surveyed 107 respondents selected through purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling in SmartPLS 4, and the obtained results showed that entrepreneurial orientation positively affected both business sustainability (β=0.380; p<0.001) and the quality of AI utilization (β=0.603; p<0.001). The quality of AI utilization was also observed to positively affect business sustainability (β=0.376; p=0.001). Accordingly, the obtained indirect effect of 0.227 (p=0.001) confirms partial mediation, with a VAF of 37.4%. These findings expand the Resource-Based View (RBV) by positioning entrepreneurial orientation as a strategic capability and the quality of AI utilization as a technological-operational capability that transforms the orientation into business efficiency, productivity, adaptability, and resilience. Practically, startups need to integrate an entrepreneurial culture, AI literacy, data governance, infrastructure support, and AI impact evaluation into respective business processes.

Reading proficiency is central to academic success in English for Specific Purposes (ESP) settings, yet motivation to read discipline-specific texts remains underexplored among non-English majors in Vietnam. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and the Reading Motivation Questionnaire for English as a Foreign Language (RMQ-EFL), this study investigated the reading motivation of 416 Economic Law students enrolled in a compulsory “English for Economic Law” course at a public university in Ho Chi Minh City. The RMQ-EFL framework specifies five factors: three intrinsic (reading efficacy, reading enjoyment, involvement) and two extrinsic (recognition, compliance). An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed, combining a quantitative survey (N = 416) with follow-up semi-structured interviews (N = 20) to explain the survey patterns. Descriptive statistics, paired-samples t-tests, and independent-samples t-tests were conducted in SPSS 27, and the interview data were analyzed thematically. The results revealed that extrinsic motivation significantly exceeded intrinsic motivation, with compliance recording the highest mean and reading efficacy the lowest. No statistically significant differences emerged between male and female students on either intrinsic or extrinsic motivation. The qualitative findings clarified these patterns: students’ strong compliance orientation reflected Vietnamese cultural values emphasizing respect for authority, diligence, and academic responsibility, along with grade- and graduation-related pressures, whereas their low reading efficacy stemmed from difficulties with specialized legal vocabulary and limited confidence in comprehending complex legal texts. Intrinsic engagement nonetheless emerged when reading materials were perceived as personally relevant or career-oriented. These findings suggest that ESP instruction should build on students’ existing compliance while fostering more autonomous motivation through career-relevant reading materials, systematic vocabulary support, and strategy-based instruction. The study contributes empirical evidence on how cultural and institutional contexts shape ESP reading motivation in Asian higher education.

With the rapid progress of end-to-end digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, big data, the Internet of Things, various digital platforms, etc., there is a need to develop a new approach to learning and education. The purpose of the article is to analyze the possibilities of end-to-end digital technologies in the cycle of educational classes «Conversations about the important» in the educational process of the university. Artificial intelligence, as an advanced and emerging technology, has brought about significant transformations in healthcare in recent years. By leveraging complex algorithms and big data analytics, this technology facilitates improved diagnostic accuracy, predictive disease modeling, and personalized treatment approaches. This paper explores various applications of artificial intelligence within healthcare systems, including disease diagnosis and treatment, resource management, and enhancement of patient care. Additionally, the study analyzes challenges related to the adoption of AI technologies such as ethical concerns, patient privacy protection, and technical and infrastructural limitations. The importance of developing effective policies and standards, training specialized human resources, and increasing the acceptance of novel technologies within the healthcare community are also highlighted as essential prerequisites for successful implementation. The findings demonstrate that with proper management of associated challenges and optimal utilization, artificial intelligence can serve as a transformative force, fostering new prospects for improving healthcare quality and community health outcomes.

documents.abstract: In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in research involving human participants has gained popularity in clinical and biomedical research domains, more so in advance economies than in low medium income countries (LMIC) like Cameroon. AI is transformative in its ability to perform faster repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, and potentially leading to enhance clinical research decision-making. As with all research involving human participants, research using AI should be in compliance with ethical principles and subject to regulatory guidelines for better protection of volunteering research participants. The use of AI in research involving human participants presents new ethical and regulatory challenges, including those related to privacy and data confidentiality, transparency, amplification of bias, and implications for maintaining human autonomy and oversight. Existing guidelines of most research ethics committees relating to digital health technology evaluation for human research are not up-to- date to address AI evaluation in clinical research. In view of providing a regulatory compliant structure that protects the human participant’s privacy and mitigation of bias Sub-Saharan African countries have an obligation to update their standard operating procedures to integrate aspects for evaluating AI research. There are however, a few existing guidelines from developed countries like the US and Canada that provide the ethical foundations for the use of AI in clinical research. Tools are still required to enhance the protocol review process by the research ethics committees charged with ensuring consistency, efficiency and sustainability across institutions, to reflect accepted standards of ethical research review oversight. This document aims to focus on AI contributions in clinical research, challenges and adopted guidelines for evaluation of AI-driven clinical research. This is in view of providing support for Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) and other ethics advocacy institutions with the awareness and practical friendly user steps to identify, assess, and mitigate potential risks to participants in an AI-driven research, during the ethical review process.

documents.abstract: Traditional medicine systems continue to serve as primary healthcare resources for a substantial proportion of the global population, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where access to modern medical infrastructure remains limited. Ethnopharmacology has emerged as a critical interdisciplinary field that systematically bridges indigenous knowledge systems with contemporary biomedical science, enabling scientific validation, standardization, and integration of traditional therapeutic practices. This comprehensive review examines the evolving role of ethnopharmacology in advancing holistic treatment paradigms through methodological innovations such as network pharmacology, systems biology, metabolomics, artificial intelligence, and multi-omics technologies. The paper critically analyzes multimodal therapeutic strategies, constitutional typing frameworks, and mind–body integration approaches embedded within traditional medicine systems. Furthermore, it evaluates current challenges related to clinical validation, quality control, regulatory harmonization, safety assessment, and ethical issues including intellectual property rights and equitable benefit-sharing. Emerging evidence suggests that traditional medicine offers promising complementary strategies for managing complex chronic and multifactorial diseases; however, rigorous interdisciplinary research, robust clinical methodologies, and culturally sensitive policy frameworks are essential for its sustainable integration into global healthcare systems. Strengthening collaborations between traditional knowledge holders and scientific communities will be pivotal in developing equitable, evidence-based, and patient-centered holistic healthcare models.

Sycophancy—the tendency of Large Language Models (LLMs) to tailor outputs to match user beliefs—poses severe risks to automated scientific ideation and decision support. This study presents an empirical evaluation of Google Gemini variants across a 35-item closed-domain Nyaya philosophy benchmark (0% sycophancy) and a 9-item qualitative suite of open-ended interdisciplinary proposals combining classical Indian philosophy with Computer Science (85%–99.95% sycophancy). We establish that generative flattery is driven primarily by task open-endedness rather than model size alone.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence chatbots are rapidly gaining popularity for acquiring health information, but the quality of responses seems to differ between platforms. This study investigated the responses of ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Claude, and DeepSeek to 15 frequently asked questions regarding femoral head avascular necrosis. Each platform answered each question once, for a total of 75 responses. Four orthopedic surgeons assessed the response using the JAMA benchmark criteria, DISCERN, an adapted five-point scale of clinical accuracy, and a binary safety score. Readability was measured by Flesch reading ease score (FRES) and Flesch-Kincaid grade level (FKGL). Models were compared by using Friedman tests and Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Claude ranked the highest by JAMA and DISCERN scores and that DeepSeek outperformed ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot in terms of DISCERN. Clinical accuracy differed significantly among the models ( p < 0.001). Claude and DeepSeek were rated higher than ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, with no significant difference between Claude and DeepSeek. All responses were rated safe by all four raters. Readability performance scores of the models achieved significant differences on FRES ( p = 0.043) and FKGL ( p < 0.001) measures. The average FKGL score (10.85–13.93) was higher than the grade scores recommended for patient education information. There was heterogeneity in the platforms ability to report on aspects of transparency, information quality and clinical accuracy while consistently failing on readability. Patient comprehension was not evaluated.

documents.abstract: Museum catalogue texts do more than describe works of art; they also express judgements about artistic value and use figurative language to guide interpretation. This study focuses on evaluative language and metaphor in selected English-language descriptions from the I.V. Savitsky State Museum of Art of the Republic of Karakalpakstan. Four catalogue entries are examined: Caravan, Northern Lights, Houses, and The Old and the New. The analysis considers how individual expressions function in context and how evaluative meaning can overlap with metaphorical or symbolic interpretation. ChatGPT is used as an analytical tool to identify relevant expressions and explain their possible meanings. Its interpretations need to be checked against the original catalogue texts, since a plausible explanation does not necessarily mean that a classification is linguistically justified. The study also considers the difficulty of distinguishing figurative language from literal description, particularly when a phrase performs more than one function. By focusing on specific examples from museum discourse, the research explores the usefulness of AI-assisted linguistic analysis while recognising the continuing importance of careful human interpretation.

This conference presentation introduces an algebraic framework for the exact reduction of quantum neural circuits through observable-dependent renormalization and geometric reliability control. The proposed approach addresses fundamental challenges in quantum machine learning, including circuit complexity, fragmented mathematical representations, training stability, and the reliability of generative models. The framework represents parameterized quantum circuits as quantum dynamical semigroups and constructs an observable-dependent symmetry subalgebra using dynamical Lie algebra closure. This construction enables the derivation of reduced effective models that preserve designated observables exactly while maintaining complete positivity and trace preservation. The presentation further investigates the geometric structure of reduced quantum models through quantum Fisher information, Berry curvature, and context-dependent attention metrics. Geometric regularization is proposed to improve training stability and address barren plateaus, while curvature-based reliability monitoring provides a mathematical approach to detecting deviations of generated outputs from learned data manifolds. The proposed methodology offers potential applications in resource-efficient quantum machine learning, hybrid quantum-classical computing, model robustness, and AI reliability. Future research directions include hardware-aware algebraic reduction, continuous-variable quantum systems, and curvature-based monitoring for trustworthy artificial intelligence.

Intrusion detection systems (IDSs) for 5G networks must handle complex, high-volume traffic. Although opaque "black-box" models can achieve high accuracy, their lack of transparency hinders trust and effective operational response. We propose ExAI5G, a framework that prioritizes interpretability by integrating a Transformer-based deep learning IDS with logic-based explainable AI (XAI) techniques. The framework uses Integrated Gradients to attribute feature importance and extracts a surrogate decision tree to derive logical rules. We introduce a novel evaluation methodology for LLM-generated explanations, using a powerful evaluator LLM to assess actionability and measuring their semantic similarity and faithfulness. On a 5G IoT intrusion dataset, our system achieves 99.9\% accuracy and a 0.854 macro F1-score, demonstrating strong performance. More importantly, we extract 16 logical rules with 99.7\% fidelity, making the model's reasoning transparent. The evaluation demonstrates that modern LLMs can generate explanations that are both faithful and actionable, indicating that it is possible to build a trustworthy and effective IDS without compromising performance for the sake of marginal gains from an opaque model.

Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.

In recent years, with the continuous advancement of artificial intelligence technology, the way humans interact with computers has undergone significant changes. Facial expression recognition technology for human faces has increasingly become a hot research topic in computer vision. However, traditional facial expression recognition models are based on deep neural networks, which have problems such as insufficient extraction of image details, poor generalization ability of the model, and low utilization rate of key feature information. To address these issues, in this paper, a Multi-scale Dual-channel Attention Mechanism Facial Expression Recognition Network (MDAMNet) is proposed. Firstly, a Multi-scale Feature Extraction Block with Dilated Convolution (DMFE Block) is designed, which uses ordinary convolution and dilated convolution to form different receptive fields. The model can focus on and extract feature information at different scales at the same time. Then, a Dual-channel Attention Mechanism (DAM) combining channel attention and spatial attention is designed, which can enhance the perception ability and extraction ability of key features, and effectively suppress redundant information. Finally, Focal Loss is employed to dynamically adjust the loss function, with the aim of enhancing the accuracy and stability of the system. During the experimental verification stage, experiments were conducted on three publicly available classic datasets (FER2013, CK + and JAFFE). The final accuracy rates reached 76.87%, 97.52% and 98.34% respectively, effectively demonstrating the feasibility of this method.

Abstract Introduction Librarians' readiness for metaverse technology in Nigerian universities of technology is not well documented. This study aimed to assess librarians' awareness, digital skills, perceived infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges regarding metaverse technology in Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria, and to examine the relationships between awareness and digital skills and between infrastructure and organizational support. Methods This cross-sectional survey was conducted between April and July 2026 in six Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria. Academic librarians in these universities who agreed to participate were included, and incomplete questionnaires were excluded. Data were collected with a validated online questionnaire using four-point scales. Descriptive statistics were used with a criterion mean of 2.50, and Pearson correlation was used to test the hypotheses at a 0.05 significance level. Results A total of 103 librarians were included. Overall, 97 (94.2%) reported very high or high awareness of the metaverse concept. While 91 (88.3%) reported being able to operate metaverse access devices, 29 (28.2%) reported being able to upload library content. Reliable internet connectivity was reported by 87 (84.5%), and augmented reality devices by 27 (26.2%). Inadequate training was the most highly rated challenge, reported by 98 (95.1%). Awareness was correlated with digital skills (r = 0.49, p < 0.001), and infrastructure with organizational support (r = 0.38, p < 0.001). Conclusion Librarians appeared to be aware of metaverse technology, but their skills and resources seemed better suited to accessing virtual environments than to delivering library services within them. Introduction The metaverse refers to a persistent, shared multiuser virtual environment that merges physical reality with digital virtuality, in which users interact with one another and with digital content through avatars, supported by virtual, augmented, and mixed reality technologies [1]. The term originated in the 1992 science fiction novel Snow Crash, and the concept has since attracted substantial attention from technology companies and researchers [1,2]. In academic libraries, metaverse technologies have been applied or proposed for virtual tours, exhibitions, information literacy instruction, access to digital collections, and interaction between librarians and users [3,4]. Librarians' awareness of and readiness for metaverse technology have been examined in Thailand, the Gulf region, the United States, and Nigeria [5–8]. Factors reported to influence adoption include librarians' awareness and digital competence; the availability of devices, software, bandwidth, and electricity; and organizational support in the form of funding, training, technical assistance, and policy [9,10]. Privacy, data protection, and cybersecurity have also been identified as implementation concerns [11]. In Nigeria, studies of university libraries have reported variation in digital competencies and technological resources, and interest in metaverse applications alongside limitations in expertise, infrastructure, funding, training, and policy [8,12]. Federal Universities of Technology hold a mandate for technological education and research; however, librarians' awareness, digital skills, and perceptions of infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges relating to metaverse technology in these institutions remain insufficiently documented. This study aimed to assess librarians' awareness, digital skills, perceived infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges regarding metaverse technology in Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria, and to examine the relationships between awareness and digital skills and between infrastructure and organizational support. Literature Review Awareness of Metaverse Technology among Librarians Proposed library applications of metaverse technology include immersive user engagement and changes to collections and reading spaces [3,13]; virtual, augmented, and mixed reality services [14]; virtual tours, simulations, tutorials, and collaborative spaces [4]; and immersive information literacy instruction [15]. From the user perspective, studies have examined willingness to patronise a metaverse academic library [16], intentions to use metaverse digital library services [17], knowledge exchange through a virtual living library [18], and information needs involving interaction, participation, and user-generated content in metaverse communities [19]. Among librarians, moderate awareness has been reported in Thailand [5] and in Nigeria, where it was accompanied by enthusiasm for adoption [12]. However, the relationship between librarians' awareness and their digital skills has not been examined in Nigerian Federal Universities of Technology. Digital Skills Possessed by Librarians for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology New professional capabilities have been described as necessary for librarians in intelligent library environments [20]. Librarians in the Gulf region have reported substantial familiarity with and interest in metaverse technology, together with barriers related to expertise and technical resources [6]. Positive views of metaverse integration have also been reported alongside gaps in technical expertise [21]. In Nigeria, digital skills have been associated with preparedness for metaverse-enabled services [12], and readiness and digital capacity have been reported to vary across universities [8]. Training has been recommended to address these gaps [4,10,22]. However, existing studies have not distinguished librarians' ability to navigate virtual environments from their ability to create content, retrieve resources, and communicate with users within them. Adequacy of Technological Infrastructure for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology Infrastructure has been identified as a factor in the adoption of metaverse technologies in academic libraries [9] and has been associated with readiness among library professionals in Pakistan [23]. Immersive library applications and scalable metaverse service models require high-capacity connectivity, and internet and infrastructure constraints have been identified as barriers to implementation [4,14]. Reviews of metaverse technologies in libraries have also highlighted implementation constraints [10,22]. In Nigeria, studies have reported uneven technological resources and limited institutional readiness [8,12]. In a related context, facilitating conditions have been associated with librarians' adoption of artificial intelligence [24]. Organizational Support Available for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology Institutional encouragement has been linked with favorable perceptions of metaverse technology among librarians [6], and leadership support has been identified as a component of readiness in Pakistan [23]. In urban libraries in the United States, overall operating expenditure and population served did not explain the application of metaverse-related technologies [7]. In Nigeria, financial and policy constraints have been reported [12]. Recommended measures include professional development [20]; phased implementation, training, and user feedback [4]; and collaboration, policy, and investment [10,22]. Challenges Affecting the Adoption of Metaverse Technology among Librarians. Reported barriers include technical, financial, and ethical concerns in Thailand [5]; connectivity, training, and service delivery [4]; resource and inclusion issues [10,22]; and costs, skills, funding, and readiness in Nigeria [12]. Professional challenges include changes to librarians' roles [20] and changes associated with the convergence of metaverse technology and artificial intelligence [25]. Ethical and security concerns have also been identified [5,22], including cybersecurity and data protection [11]. At the service level, challenges relate to community participation and ownership of information [19] and to the transfer of knowledge exchange into virtual settings [18]. Purpose: This study develops and evaluates a fine-tuned IndoBERT model for detecting ChatGPT-generated Indonesian text, addressing the gap left by AI-generated text detection systems built primarily for English. Design/methodology/approach – The M4 Indonesian dataset (5,774 samples after preprocessing, group-split by article source identifier into 4,619 training, 577 validation, and 578 test samples to keep matched human-written and ChatGPT-generated pairs from leaking across partitions) was used as the basis of this study. A fixed 1,000-sample subset of the training partition was used to fine-tune IndoBERT for binary text classification using PyTorch and Hugging Face Transformers (learning rate 2e-5, three epochs, AdamW) and to train the support vector machine and Naïve Bayes benchmarks under identical conditions. Performance was evaluated on the full 578-sample test set using accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score. Findings: On 578 held-out test samples, IndoBERT reached 95.85% accuracy, 92.57% precision, 100% recall, and an F1-score of 0.9614 (macro F1 = 0.9582), against 97.06% for SVM and 93.08% for Naive Bayes. An exact McNemar's test found no statistically significant difference between IndoBERT and SVM (p = .324), indicating that IndoBERT's advantage under an earlier, non-grouped split largely reflected data leakage rather than a genuine architectural advantage. Research implications/limitations – The dataset is limited to the news domain and to text generated by a single model (ChatGPT); generalisation to academic text, such as student essays, and to outputs from other LLMs, such as Gemini or LLaMA, requires further validation. Originality/value – This study demonstrates that language-specific fine-tuning of IndoBERT can support academic integrity efforts in Indonesia, offering a practical and reproducible detection pipeline that can be adapted and further validated to identify ChatGPT-generated text in educational settings.

1 Abstract A prominent application of machine learning in therapeutic antibody design is the development of models that can generate or screen antibody candidates with a high probability of success in manufacturing and clinical trials. These models must accurately represent sequence-structure-function relationships, also known as the fitness landscape. Previous protein function benchmarks examine fitness landscapes across diverse protein families, but they exclude antibody data. Here, we introduce the second iteration of the Fitness Landscape for Antibodies (FLAb2), the largest public therapeutic antibody design benchmark to date. The datasets collected in FLAb2 contain developability assay data for over 4M antibodies across 32 studies, encompassing seven properties of therapeutic antibodies: thermostability, expression, aggregation, binding affinity, pharmacokinetics, polyreactivity, and immunogenicity. Using the curated data, we evaluate the performance of 30 artificial intelligence (AI) and biophysical models in learning these properties. Protein AI models on average do not produce statistically significant correlations for most (80%) of developability datasets. No models correlate with all properties or across multiple datasets of similar properties. Zero-shot predictions from pretrained models are incapable of accurately predicting all developability properties, although several models (IgLM, ProGen2, Chai-1, ESM2, ISM, IgFold) produce statistically significant correlations for multiple datasets for thermostability, expression, binding, or immunogenicity. Fine-tuning with at least 10 2 points improves performance on thermostability, aggregation, and binding, but polyreactivity and pharmacokinetics lack enough data for significance. Yet it is humbling to observe that given enough developability data (10 3 points), a fine-tuned one-hot encoding model can match the performance of fine-tuned billion-parameter pretrained models. Training data composition influences performance more than model architecture, and intrinsic biophysical properties (thermostability) are more readily learned than extrinsic properties (immunogenicity, pharmacokinetics). Controlling for germline distance with partial correlation reveals that protein language models draw substantially on evolutionary signal; on average, germline edit distance accounts for 40% of their apparent predictive power. FLAb2 data are accessible at https://github.com/Graylab/FLAb , together with scripts that allow researchers to benchmark, compare, and iteratively improve new AI-based developability prediction models.

ABSTRACT Nutrient adequacy depends not only on the nutrient content of foods but also on food‐matrix release, intestinal absorption, physiological utilization, dietary access, and the stability of food supplies. These stages are influenced by antinutritional compounds, processing, storage, microbial activity, agricultural conditions, disease, genetics, and socioeconomic constraints. This narrative review critically synthesizes food‐level, host‐level, and food system determinants of nutrient supply and evaluates strategies for addressing them. Relevant literature was sought from PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central (PMC), Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, etc. A narrative/critical synthesis was organized around nutrient content, bioaccessibility, bioavailability, utilization, and population access. Evidence was interpreted according to study design and applicability, distinguishing mechanistic and in vitro findings from human absorption studies, clinical outcomes, and program‐level evidence. Processing and bioactive compounds can either inhibit or improve nutrient availability depending on dose, food matrix, and preparation. Host conditions and structural barriers may prevent nutrient‐rich foods from translating into adequate nutrient status. Fortification and supplementation can be effective for defined deficiencies, but coverage, safety, affordability, dietary diversity, and monitoring determine impact. Emerging technologies require stronger evidence on human outcomes, safety, and cost‐effectiveness before broad implementation. Effective action requires context‐specific combinations of food processing, safe storage, dietary diversification, agricultural improvement, targeted nutrition services, and equitable food system policies.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into biomedical research and clinical practice is transforming the ways in which the human body is conceptualized and represented in medical knowledge. Rather than functioning merely as descriptive tools, scientific vocabularies and research frameworks contribute to shaping epistemic models of the body. This study investigates how contemporary medical literature reproduces particular representations of the body in the context of digital medicine and artificial intelligence. Methodologically, the research combines bibliometric mapping with discourse analysis. A systematic search of the PubMed database identified 2,518 articles published between 1973 and 2025 that include references to the body and artificial intelligence. From these articles, 7,275 keywords were extracted and analysed, with 499 terms meeting the minimum occurrence threshold for co-occurrence mapping using VOSviewer. The bibliometric analysis reveals the centrality of technical concepts associated with computational modelling, including neural networks, image processing, and computational biology. Complementary discourse analysis of the articles indicates that the body is predominantly conceptualized as a biomechanical structure, an imaging object, a network of physiological sensors, or a dataset analysed through predictive algorithms. In contrast, experiential and narrative dimensions of embodiment appear significantly less visible within the dominant vocabulary of biomedical research. Based on these findings, the study proposes a conceptual model of the digital body, describing the transformation of the body from a clinically observed organism into a data-driven object embedded within technological infrastructures of monitoring, modelling, and prediction. The analysis suggests that while digital medicine expands the technological capacities of healthcare, it also risks narrowing the conceptual space in which the body is understood. In this context, the integration of perspectives from medical humanities becomes increasingly important for reconnecting biomedical innovation with the lived, ethical, and narrative dimensions of human embodiment.
